newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German car industry faces slower growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German car industry faces slower growth.

text.p: The German car industry faces a delicate year in 1997 with production likely to grow more slowly than last year and with increasing dependence on exports, the president of the VDA German Auto Association said on Wednesday.

In his annual press conference on the state of the German car industry, Bernd Gottschalk said car production this year would grow between two to three percent, a slowdown from 4.1 percent growth in 1996.

"The car year 1997 has potential, but it will be anything other than self-sustaining," Gottschalk said. "Uncertainty and risk are not to be underestimated and could cloud the good prospects for the auto industry."
Expectations of slower growth in 1997 are the latest sign of a slowdown here in the sector after the market rebounded strongly from a disappointing global car market in 1993.
The VDA president said the fundamentals for growth are in place with German carmakers expected to increase investment by five percent this year and producing models well received in the market place.
But slow economic growth at home, high labour costs and tax burdens could yet wear on the nation's car industry.
The key to growth may lie outside Germany's borders where economic growth is expected to be stronger and where German carmakers have made strong inroads.
Last year, German firms boosted their share of the global car market to 14.7 percent from 14.2 percent the year before.
"We should not forget that outside the current muted mood in Germany, a majority of our trading partners expect a continuation of economic growth," Gottschalk said.
The VDA chief, however, warned that foreign demand will be anything but robust and could even fall in some cases.
Gottschalk said top priorities for the German car industry are to reduce costs and taxes.
German labour costs at 62 marks an hour are nearly double France's 33 marks an hour and well ahead of Britain's 27 marks.
German carmakers, unable to cut labour costs fast, continued to cut their domestic workforces and move output abroad.
In 1996, the German firms reduced the total size of the workforce by 0.6 percent to 657,100 employees. The car industry workforce had hit a peak in 1991 of more than 760,000 workers.

The tax burden faced by German carmakers is also the highest among its major European competitors and Gottschalk called for Bonn to cut the taxes which hinder investment such as the trade tax on capital and capital gains tax.
Gottschalk, who headed the truck division at Mercedes-Benz AG before taking over the VDA, said commercial vehicles are showing early signs of recovery.

The German truck market, especially for large vehicles, has suffered under stiff competition from Swedish makers like Volvo and a weak building sector that reduces the need for heavy transportation vehicles.
The VDA chief forecast four percent growth in truck production after a decline of one percent in 1996. "We still will be at an unsatisfying level, especially in heavy trucks," he said.
